posts.title: Roadside Atlas #1: Teapot Dome Gas Station — Zillah’s Political Landmark
posts.summary: A 1922 teapot-shaped roadside landmark built in Zillah, Washintgon, as a reminder of the Teapot Dome scandal.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1987, this is the Teapot Dome Service Station in Zillah, Washington. Built in 1922 on U.S. Route 12, the teapot-shaped station was created as a visual reminder of the Teapot Dome scandal and is now located at 117 First Avenue.

blocks.label: John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #2: Wadhams Pagoda Station — Milwaukee’s Red-Roof Relic
posts.summary: This 1930 Wadhams pagoda-style gas station in Milwaukee was later known as the Harley Sprague Mobil Station and became one of the city’s memorable roadside landmarks.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1977, this is the former Wadhams Oil Co. / Clinton Street Filling Station, later known as the Harley Sprague Mobil Station, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Built in 1930 and designed by architect Alexander C. Eschweiler, it was one of Wadhams’ distinctive pagoda-style gas stations, with a bright red roof that turned a small service station into a roadside landmark. The building was later moved to 430 S. 2nd Street, then disassembled in 2002; part of the roof eventually entered the Wisconsin Historical Society Museum collection.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #3: Busan Sikdang — American and Korean Food on Route 27
posts.summary: Busan Sikdang on Route 27 in Columbus, Georgia paired classic diner architecture with Korean signage and an American/Korean menu.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1982, this Columbus, Georgia diner combined classic American roadside architecture with Korean immigrant food culture. Its Korean window lettering reads Busan Sikdang—“Busan Restaurant”—while the hand-painted English signs advertise “American and Korean Food,” turning a small streamliner-style diner on Route 27 into a vivid record of roadside adaptation and cultural overlap.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #4: Lucy the Elephant — Margate’s Seaside Giant
posts.summary: Lucy the Elephant is an 1881 elephant-shaped landmark in Margate City, New Jersey.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1978, this is Lucy the Elephant in Margate City, New Jersey. Built in 1881 by James V. Lafferty, the elephant-shaped building became one of America’s most recognizable examples of novelty roadside architecture, part attraction, part landmark, and part seaside lookout.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #5: Playland — Ocean City Boardwalk Fantasia
posts.summary: Playland on the Ocean City, New Jersey boardwalk captures the bright, theatrical look of an Atlantic coast amusement landmark.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1978, this is Playland on the boardwalk in Ocean City, New Jersey. The Library of Congress record identifies it as “Playland, Ocean City, New Jersey,” part of Margolies’s Roadside America documentation of Atlantic coast amusements and vernacular commercial architecture. The shuttered stands, painted dome, “King’s Tomb” sign, and boardwalk food counters capture the theatrical off-season face of a seaside amusement strip.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #6: Barrel-N-Bun — Wildwood’s Barrel-Shaped Boardwalk Stand
posts.summary: Barrel-N-Bun was a whimsical Wildwood boardwalk food stand, turning hot dogs and hamburgers into a playful seaside landmark.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1978, this is the Barrel-N-Bun hot dog and hamburger stand on the Wildwood, New Jersey boardwalk. Its oversized barrel form, rooftop hot dog, Coca-Cola menu board, and boardwalk setting capture the novelty architecture Margolies documented across American roadside and seaside culture.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #7: Glacier Theater — Main Street Afterlife
posts.summary: Browning’s Glacier Theater shows a small-town movie house adapted into a video rental storefront.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1988, this is the Glacier Theater on Main Street in Browning, Montana. By the time Margolies documented it, the former theater facade had been repurposed for video rentals, preserving a transitional moment in movie culture: a small-town theater becoming part of the home-video era while still carrying the shape and signage of its earlier life.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #8: Rialto Theatre — Deer Lodge Movie Palace
posts.summary: Deer Lodge’s Rialto Theatre is a 1921 Beaux-Arts movie palace, remembered for its ornate terra-cotta facade.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 2004, this is the Rialto Theatre at 418 Main Street in Deer Lodge, Montana. Built in 1921 by Arnold & Van Hausen, the Beaux-Arts theater was known for its white terra-cotta facade, red tile roof, ornate columns, murals, and 720-seat auditorium. A 2006 fire gutted much of the building, but the historic facade survived; after a community-led restoration, the Rialto reopened in 2012 as a multipurpose venue for films, concerts, and live events.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #9: Miss Bellows Falls Diner — Worcester Lunch Car #771
posts.summary: Miss Bellows Falls Diner is Worcester Lunch Car #771, a 1941 barrel-roofed diner in Bellows Falls, Vermont, later listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1978, this is the Miss Bellows Falls Diner in Bellows Falls, Vermont. Built in 1941 by the Worcester Lunch Car Company as car #771, the diner is a barrel-roofed metal structure at 90 Rockingham Street, known for its porcelain enamel panels, red lettering, booth-service signage, and classic lunch-car form. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1983 and remains one of Vermont’s notable surviving roadside diners.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #10: Fox Theater — Missoula’s Neon Tower
posts.summary: Missoula’s Fox Theater is captured here through its bold vertical neon sign, a surviving trace of the city’s mid-century movie culture.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1987, this image focuses on the Fox Theater’s towering roadside-style neon sign rising above Front Street in Missoula, Montana. The bold orange-and-black “FOX” lettering, geometric metal supports, and yellow modernist marquee capture the theater less as a full building portrait than as a study in mid-century movie-house signage—built to be seen from a distance, glowing over the street like a landmark.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #11: Capt. Bob’s Bull — Ocean City’s Sunglassed Landmark
posts.summary: This giant fiberglass bull once stood outside Captain Bob’s BBQ in Ocean City, Maryland.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1985, this giant fiberglass bull stood outside Captain Bob’s BBQ in Ocean City, Maryland, where its chef’s hat, sunglasses, and bright red scarf turned a steakhouse mascot into a Delmarva roadside icon. Now remembered as “Bob the Bull,” the statue later found a new home in Delaware, carrying a piece of Ocean City’s mid-century roadside culture with it.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #12: West Theater — Route 66 Star Tower
posts.summary: The West Theater on Route 66 in Grants, New Mexico is captured through its bold vertical sign, starbursts, and mid-century marquee.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 2003, this is the West Theater on Route 66 in Grants, New Mexico. The image centers on the theater’s vertical “WEST” sign, with yellow letters, pale blue fins, and stacked starbursts rising against the desert sky. Rather than showing the full building, Margolies frames the theater through its sign and marquee: a piece of mid-century roadside movie-house design built for visibility, drama, and passing traffic.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #13: Stork Cafe — Route 66 Lunch Counter
posts.summary: The Stork Cafe was a compact Route 66 diner in Winslow, Arizona, remembered for its bold cafe signs, rooftop stork, and classic roadside lunch-counter character.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1979, this is the Stork Cafe on 3rd Street along Route 66 in Winslow, Arizona. The compact roadside diner advertises hamburgers, hot dogs, sandwiches to go, and all-day breakfast beneath bold cafe signage, with a rooftop stork adding a bit of roadside whimsy.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #14: State Theater — Central Avenue Art Deco
posts.summary: Photographed by John Margolies in 1979, Albuquerque’s State Theater on Central Avenue shows a Route 66 movie house defined by its Art Deco facade and tall vertical sign.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1979, this is the State Theater on Central Avenue, Route 66, in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The image frames the theater’s Art Deco facade and vertical red “STATE” sign, with stepped wall details, a broad marquee, and boarded entrance capturing a once-prominent movie house in a quieter later chapter.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #15: Hiland Theater — Central Avenue Streamline
posts.summary: Albuquerque’s Hiland Theater captures a 1950 Route 66 movie house through its Streamline Moderne vertical sign and glass-block tower.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1987, this is the Hiland Theater on Central Avenue / Route 66 in Albuquerque, New Mexico. The image focuses on the theater’s vertical sign, with tall “HILAND” lettering, curved Streamline Moderne edges, and pale glass-block detailing set against the blue sky. Built in 1950, the Hiland was one of Albuquerque’s postwar Route 66 movie houses, designed for the automobile era with a large rear parking lot; it stopped screening films in 1995 and later reopened as a performing arts and dance venue.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #16: Ocean City Life-Saving Station — Boardwalk Rescue House
posts.summary: the Ocean City Life-Saving Station Museum preserves an 1891 rescue station at the south end of the Ocean City, Maryland boardwalk.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies, this is the Ocean City Life-Saving Station Museum at the south end of the Ocean City, Maryland boardwalk. Built in 1891 for the U.S. Life-Saving Service, the station later served the U.S. Coast Guard until 1964 before being saved from demolition by local preservation efforts. Margolies’s image captures the restored white-and-red building as a seaside landmark, with its steep gables, lookout tower, boardwalk setting, and large anchor display emphasizing its maritime rescue history.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #17: El Rancho Theater — Pine Street Pueblo Revival
posts.summary: Deming, NZ’s El Rancho Theater pairs Pueblo Revival details with a vivid desert marquee and weathered vertical sign.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1979, this is the El Rancho Theater on Pine Street in Deming, New Mexico. The image captures the theater’s Pueblo Revival facade, with stepped parapets, projecting vigas, a weathered vertical “EL RANCHO” sign, and a painted desert landscape across the marquee.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #18: Riviera Theatre — Muscatine’s Last Marquee
posts.summary: Muscatine’s Riviera Theatre shows a former Uptown Theatre / Bosten Cinema near the end of its life, shortly before its 1990 closure and demolition.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1988, this is the Riviera Theatre in Muscatine, Iowa. The theater stood at 313 E. 3rd Street and had earlier operated as the Uptown Theatre and later Bosten Cinema before becoming the Riviera in 1983. Margolies’s image captures it near the end of its life: a brick movie house with an ornate marquee, gold scrollwork, poster cases, and “Betrayed” still listed on the sign. The theater closed in 1990 and was later demolished.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #19: Highway Diner — Route 66 Streamline
posts.summary: Winslow’s Highway Diner is a streamlined Valentine diner on Route 66, preserved as a compact red-and-white survivor of old roadside food culture.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 2003, this is the Highway Diner on Route 66 in Winslow, Arizona. Margolies described it as a survivor of old Route 66, noting its streamlined Art Deco character and its connection to the Valentine Diner Company of Wichita, Kansas, a major supplier of small diner buildings in the West and Midwest. In the image, the red-and-white exterior, striped awnings, rooftop sign, and curved gooseneck lights make the compact building feel both practical and theatrical: a short-order diner designed to catch the eye from the road.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #20: Ziggie’s Conch — Fine Food in the Keys
posts.summary: Ziggie’s the Conch was a beloved Islamorada roadside restaurant, remembered for its bright “FINE FOOD” sign and unmistakable Florida Keys character.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies in 1985, this is Ziggie’s the Conch Restaurant in Islamorada, Florida, a Florida Keys landmark remembered for its “FINE FOOD” neon sign, “Ziggie Your Host” lettering, lime green walls, mounted fish, and boat-shaped player piano. The building’s history traces back to the 1930s, before becoming Ziggie’s Conch after Ziggie Stocki purchased the property in 1962; it later became Ziggie & Mad Dog’s in 2006.
John Margolies Roadside America photograph archive, Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division.

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #21: Strömstadsvägen Service Stop, Sweden, 1930s (Colorized)
posts.summary: This Strömstadsvägen fuel station in Uddevalla shows taxis lined up.

blocks.text: Photographed by Olof Einar Lindström, this image shows a fuel station on Strömstadsvägen in Uddevalla, Sweden, operated by Bilägarnas Inköpsförening, likely in the early-to-mid 1930s. The DigitaltMuseum record notes that taxis are lined up at the station and that the site was later succeeded by OK.

blocks.label: Olof Einar Lindström / Bohusläns museum, via DigitaltMuseum

posts.title: Roadside Atlas #22: St. Simons Lighthouse Museum — Keeper’s House and Coastal Beacon
posts.summary: St. Simons Lighthouse Museum preserves an 1872 coastal beacon and keeper’s house on St. Simons Island, Georgia.

blocks.text: Photographed by John Margolies, this is the St. Simons Lighthouse Museum on St. Simons Island, Georgia. The lighthouse was first lit in 1872 and stands with the historic keeper’s dwelling, guiding ships into St. Simons Sound and marking the sandbar-filled waters off Georgia’s coast.

groupings.title: Hoichi the Earless
groupings.summary: On the quiet shores of Dan-no-ura, a blind musician is summoned to play for a mysterious audience.

posts.title: Hoichi the Earless
posts.summary: A blind musician is summoned to perform before a noble court. But the court is not of the living.

blocks.text: Many years ago, in the narrow straits at Dan-no-ura, two great clans met in a final, terrible battle. The Heike and the Genji. The Heike were destroyed, warriors and nobles pulled beneath the waves. And as their cries fell silent, the emperor's grandmother chose to drown her previous grandson, rather than let him be captured and humiliated by his enemy.
The sea remembers that day.

Fishermen still speak of strange lights drifting over the water at night—pale, flickering flames they call oni-bi. When storms roll in, the wind carries a sound like distant battle. And sometimes, in the quiet between waves, there are voices.
A temple was built to soothe the restless dead: Amidaji. Nearby, a cemetery marked the resting place of the fallen.
Prayers were offered daily.
But still, the dead were never entirely at peace.

In this place lived Hoichi. Blind from childhood, he was trained in the biwa and the recitation of history. His voice was clear, precise, expressive. When he sang of Dan-no-ura, listeners wept. It was said even the spirits could not resist his telling.

Hoichi had very little at first. But the priest of Amidaji took pity on him, providing a room, food, and shelter. In return, Hoichi played on quiet evenings, his flawless music and his perfect voice carrying over the narrow straits.
It was a simple life.
And a peaceful one.
Until the night when someone came for him.
It was a hot night in summer, the air smelling of brine and kelp, and the cicadas sounding among the pines above the temple.
The priest had been called away. Unable to sleep in the heavy air, Hoichi sat on the veranda, biwa across his lap, the garden beyond him perfectly still.
He heard footsteps approaching.
They were not hesitant. They were heavy and deliberate.
They stopped directly in front of him.
"Hoichi."
The voice was deep and commanding.
"I am blind," Hoichi replied. "I cannot see who calls."
"There is nothing to fear. My lord, a man of high rank, is staying nearby. He has heard of your gifts, Hoichi. You will come with me and perform."
Hoichi could tell that it was not a request. He was being summoned, and he dared not refuse.
Hoichi rose, took his instrument, and followed.
Metal shifted with each step of the summoner who walked in front of him. He was a warrior.
They moved quickly. Faster than Hoichi thought possible. Soon they passed through a great gate, which opened without a word.
Hoichi listened with great care as they walked. The sounds of a garden. Then onward, into the sounds of an echoing hallway, their quick steps along polished floors.
He heard voices. They were soft and refined, and to his ears, unmistakably noble, the sing-song words of Heian-kyō, the words of old poems and courtly tales from the Imperial Capital.
Hoichi heard the voices grow louder as he was guided into a large hall. He was made to sit upon a cushion, elevated on what he was certain to be stage.
A woman spoke, her voice dignified and eternal:
"You will recite for us the story of the Battle of Dan-no-ura."
He began.

The biwa came alive beneath his hands — oars cutting water, arrows splitting air, ships colliding, steel ringing against steel. His voice carried the rise and fall of battle, the chaos, the grief of inevitable defeat.
The room held its breath.

At last, Hoichi reached the final scene. The last moments of the Emperor Antoku, at only six years old. The battle lost, the house of Heike defeated. And so, the once-mighty Kiyomori's widow carries her beloved grandson into the dark waters, telling him of a palace beneath the waves, choosing death over surrender to the Genji.
There was a silence at first from his audience. Then they fell into grief, an open, unguarded, and inconsolable weeping. The men as well as the women, and even the small wailing of a young child.
Hoichi faltered. He had moved audiences before. He had never shaken a room like this.
At last, the woman spoke again.
"You will return tomorrow night. You will recite the story again."
A pause.
"Tell no one."
He was led back before dawn.
He said nothing.

sections.title: Part 3 — The Truth in the Dark

blocks.text: The summons came again.
And again.
Each night Hoichi left. And each morning he returned quieter, his body worn at the edges in a way that sleep did not repair.
The priest noticed the change. He could see his friend suffering.
But his questions received only careful, vague answers.
So the priest told two of his servants to follow him.
That night, they did, but lost him almost immediately. The sightless Hoichi moved through the dark faster than he should have been able.
The servants searched.
They found nothing. They turned back to tell their master.
But then, near the shore, they heard it: the sound of the biwa.
And they could hear the story of Dan-no-ura.
They followed the sounds to the cemetery.
Light from their lanterns fell over the headstones, and they stopped.
Between the grave markers were of pale flames drifting above the ground, hovering without wind, without source. Countless lights.
And in their center, seated before the tomb of the drowned emperor, was Hoichi.
The rain was falling around him. His voice was raised in full performance. His face turned toward nothing.
The dead were listening.
The servants seized his shoulders, shouted his name. He fought them.
"You must not interrupt," Hoichi said. "This is an august gathering!"
The servants dragged him away.
Once back at the temple, before the priest, Hoichi recounted what had been happening to him.
The priest listened without speaking, focusing on every detail of Hoichi's account.
Then:
"You have not been visiting a lord's court," the priest said.
Hoichi heard the priest pause, and almost hesitate.
"Hoichi... you have been performing for the dead of Dan-no-ura."
The priest knew that the ghosts would continue this forever, that they would never let Hoichi stop.
There was only one way to protect him.

Before nightfall, the priest and an assistant prepared Hoichi. They cut his hair and shaved his head. They then covered Hoichi's body in sacred text — sutras written in careful strokes across every surface. Chest, back, face, hands, feet, the backs of his fingers.
"These will hide you", the priest said. "Do not speak. Do not move. No matter what you hear."
The night came and Hoichi waited.
He was still and silent, as the priest had instructed.
He heard the heavy footsteps.
The gate.
The garden.
And now, his summoner, directly in front of him.
"Hoichi."
He did not answer.
"Hoichi."
He was silent.
A third time — sharper, irritated.
Hoichi kept himself still.
The figure moved closer. Hoichi heard the shift of armored weight, the soft displacement of air. Felt the presence of something immense and very old leaning over him.
When the voice came again, it was almost to itself:
"I see the instrument…"
A pause.
"…but the player—"
Hoichi could feel something changed in the air.
"There is nothing here."
The pause that followed had the quality of a held breath.
"Nothing..."
Hoichi dared not take a breath.
"Aside from the ears."
Hoichi held firm as the summoner seized them.
It was hard. Violent. Final.
And then they were gone.
Hoichi did not cry out.
He did not move.
And the summoner left.
At dawn, the priest found him where he had been left — seated on the veranda, the floor beneath him dark and wet.
The priest was his simple mistake.
The sutras had covered his body.
But not his ears.
But Hoichi had survived, and his wounds healed.
People came from distant places to hear him — not just for the skill that had always been extraordinary, but for what that skill had cost.
Hoichi was famous. He continued to recite The Tale of the Heike, and brought his listeners to tears when he recounted the Battle of Dan-no-ura, and told of the palace beneath the waves.
By that time, he was known by a new name: Hoichi the Earless.

And with each full moon, Hoichi would sit facing the cemetery with his biwa, and recite the opening passages of the tale — the temple bells of Gion, the blossoms of the sala trees — offering to the young Emperor what he could give, and the only thing the boy had never been given: a gentle story.
